translations.title: On the Ages of Women
translations.text:
From fifteen to twenty she is a girl; a fine lass from twenty to twenty-five, and by the reckoning a gracious woman from twenty-five to thirty. Happy he who enjoys her at such an age!

From thirty to thirty-five she brings no joy; but may be eaten with salt and pepper; yet from thirty-five to forty she is already on the eve of disgrace.

At forty-five she is a learned scold, speaks through her nose, begs and toys with words; and once fifty is reached, she turns holy,

and at fifty-five sets up her shrine. Girl, lass, woman, crone, enchantress, witch and holy woman—the devil carries her off.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Consumed in Earth, Though Not in Fame
translations.text:
Consumed in earth, though not in fame, you lie, O life, the more feared, cast down from purple to marble, opened by a wound to tears more than blood.

Now mourned by all who feared you, respected by the world, not fate; in you, by vilely wielding a bloody sword, one life took so many from death.

When in a thousand victories it presumes to stain fields and redden seas, naked centers of envious glories,

a traitor clothes the ground with its spoils: its lily with horror; memories with example; hands with idleness; eyes with pity.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: To Aminta, Who Covered Her Eyes with Her Hand...
translations.text:
If He Who Must Paint You Must See You...\nIf he who must paint you must see you, and none can look without going blind, who will be able to portray you without offending his sight and you?

I wished to make you bloom in snow and roses; but that would honor roses and wrong you; I wished to give you two stars for eyes; but when did stars ever dream of it?

I knew the sketch impossible; but your mirror, by your own light, assured success in its reflection.

It can portray you without borrowed light, since in the mirror you yourself are original, painter, brush, and copy.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Now, Laura, Your Window Rests
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Constant Love Beyond Death
translations.text:
The final shadow may close my eyes and carry off the white day, and an hour flattering its anxious yearning may unbind this soul of mine;

but on the farther shore memory will not leave where it burned: my flame knows how to swim cold water and lose respect for stern law.

Soul whom a whole god imprisoned, veins that gave fluid to so much fire, marrow that has gloriously burned:

they will leave their body, not their care; they will be ashes, yet will feel; they will be dust, yet dust in love.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: From the Tower
translations.text:
Withdrawn in the peace of these solitudes, with few but learned books together, I converse with the departed and listen with my eyes to the dead.

Though not always understood, always open, they correct or enrich my affairs; and in silent musical counterpoint they speak awake to life's sleep.

The great souls death removes, learned printing, avenger of the injuries of years, frees, O great Don Josef.

The hour flees irretrievably; but best reckons the hour that improves us through reading and study.


We thank Francisco Larrión Riveroll for suggesting this poem for the Ciudad Seva Digital Library.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Whoever Would Be Cultured in a Single Day...
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Lyrical Refrain
translations.text:
What use, rosebush, is boasting of beauty, if scarcely born you begin to die? Your blush, alive and dead, makes us weep and laugh in one day or one sun: from East to sunset your beauty passes in one step, your perfection in less. Rosebush, boast less among the pinks, for tomorrow those now roses will be thorns.

Your rank gives no great advantage: if dawn is your mantle, night is your shroud. No flower is so lowly it will not outlive you, and the mallow, hair of a clod, laughs at your pretensions as dawn's descendant. Rosebush, boast less among the pinks, for tomorrow those now roses will be thorns.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: On the Pain of Being in Love
translations.text:
What true pain, what refined suffering! What a lying life! What pure death from love!

What cares by the thousand! What clashes of opinions! What limited pleasures, what overflowing griefs!

What love and lack of love! What offenses, what endurance! What a lying life, what pure death from love!

What accepted follies! What beloved displeasures! What daring thoughts and cowardly desires!

What adored disfavor! What silent suffering! What a lying life! What pure death from love!

What negotiated deceits and forced torments! What hated breaths and desired injuries!

What courage and what fear! What blindness, what foreseeing! What a lying life! What pure death from love!

What entanglements, anguish, assaults, what harmonious opposites! What wisdom, what recklessness! What a life of shocks!

And no death is greater than possessing it and not dying. What a lying life! What pure death from love!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: What Do You Capture, Nocturnal, in Your Songs?
translations.text:
What do you capture, nocturnal, in your songs, foolish Góngora, by twilighting them, if when you most yearn to heron-flight them, you reptilize and underpose them more?

God microcosmed you with inquisitions, and you want them to investigate you by medals as ancient signs or antiquities, to unroute apprentice bards.

Your foreignness is so eminent that whoever ruminates you must detract you, for you belch visceral cacochymy,

pharmaco-coloring like a mummy, if you give such slight stomach-abundance, metamorphosing arcadumy.

Yesterday was a dream; tomorrow will be earth! A moment before, nothing; a moment after, smoke! I assign ambitions and presume scarcely a point within the circle closing me!

Brief combat of troublesome war: in my defense I am the greatest danger; while my weapons consume me, the body lodges me less than buries me.

Yesterday is gone; tomorrow has not arrived; today passes, is, and was, in a motion hurling me toward death.

Hour and instant are spades that, paid by my pain and care, dig my monument in my life.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: To a Pair of Legs
translations.text:
O ivory bases, living building made by heaven's craftsman, alabaster columns that give us on earth clear proof of supreme good!

Beautiful capitals and workmanship of the arch that makes even me jealous! Altar where the young tyrant god would sacrifice himself!

O gate of Cupid's glory and guardian of the most prized flower ever in the world!

Let us know how long you remain closed and the crystalline heaven defended from one who never tasted forbidden fruit.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: I Dreamed I Was Thrown from a Cliff
translations.text:
I dreamed the one who held my love subject to herself threw me from a cliff, and a beast waiting below almost caught me in its mouth.

Fearfully I sought something my hands could hold: one grasped a sword's edge and the other dug into a little plant.

The plant was swiftly uprooted, the sword was destroying my hand, and I pressed its living edges harder...

O wretched me, how poorly I understand myself, for I delight to see myself torn apart from fear of ending my pain by dying!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Two Goats Are Gnawing a Knotted Branch
translations.text:
Two goats gnaw a knotted, hard, dry branch in the willow, for in green spring it was sweet, soft, tender, and delicious to them.

They find the taste strange and bitter, no good branch along the bank, for as its season passed, so did its delightful taste.

Missing that flavor, they bite from branch to branch and stubbornly remain unfed.

Memories of my sweet good days, so I wander after you, seeing nothing but ended joys!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Leave the Curls of Gold
translations.text:
Leave the curls of gold that hold my soul entwined, and return to untrodden snow the white tinged by those roses.

Leave the pearls and precious coral adorning that mouth, and return to envious heaven the suns you stole from it.

Return the grace and discretion shown by the heavenly Master's great wisdom to angelic nature;

and all this restored, you will see what remains truly yours: to be harsh, cruel, ungrateful, and hard.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Let Me
translations.text: If rain's smallest fingers tremble on your face and slide; if the light cloak of the breeze wraps you; if the mirror smiles whenever you look at it; and many breasts rise from the sea toward the clear light of warm hands; let my fingers draw your image in a long, trembling caress; let my arms encircle your shoulders with a sharp, possessive bearing; let my face float in the radiant dark circles of your pupils; and grant full freedom to these hands that long to make you mine.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Embraces
translations.text: Let Me\nIf rain's smallest fingers tremble on your face and slide; if the light cloak of the breeze wraps you; if the mirror smiles whenever you look at it; and many breasts rise from the sea toward the clear light of warm hands; let my fingers draw your image in a long, trembling caress; let my arms encircle your shoulders with a sharp, possessive bearing; let my face float in the radiant dark circles of your pupils; and grant full freedom to these hands that long to make you mine.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Song
translations.text:
Returning from harsh prison where I nearly left my life, fortune in its unreason still rages at me, hates me, and does not forget. Its sting could be satisfied with so many wounds upon my return.

If in its unreason it wants nothing less than seeing me lifeless, may God grant my heart shelter in His heaven upon my return!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Lay or Rondel of Death
translations.text:
Death, I appeal against your rigor: you took my beloved from me, yet were not sated, and robbed me of all ardor, leaving me here without strength. My living did you no harm, Death!

We were two and a single heart; if she died, I too must die, or perhaps live without life, like a phantom in imagination. Death!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad of the Fair Armorer to the Young Courtesans
translations.text:
Consider, fair Glover, once my pupil, and Blanche the Shoemaker, that you must learn to live. Take left and right—God sent each passing man—for an old woman is discarded like a coin no longer current.

And you, lovely Sausage Seller whose dancing banishes sleep, and Guillemette the Tapestry Maker: satisfy the master's whims! Soon this time will be far away, you will be ugly as owls, of no use even to old priests, like a coin no longer current.

You, Jeannette the Hatmaker: let no love detain you; you, Catherine the Pursemaker: scorn no man who comes; though, remembering myself, I sometimes smile and urge them on, I know no one will take me, like a coin no longer current.

Know, girls, that if I burst into such sad, abundant tears, it is because I find no one to seek me, like a coin no longer current.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad of the Lords of Former Times
translations.text:
Where is Callixtus the Third, pope for four years, the last of that name to die? And gracious Charles of Bourbon, Arthur, Duke of Brittany, Alfonso reigning in Aragon, and triumphant Charles the Seventh? But where is bold Charlemagne?

And Scotland's king, said to have one cheek blood-red from forehead to below his lips? And the valiant king of Spain whose name I have forgotten? And the famous king of Cyprus? But where is bold Charlemagne?

I forgo speaking of vanished glories: the world is only a vain dream. None triumphs over death; palaces do not stop it. One question still: that Bohemian king, Ladislaus—where is he, where his grandfather? But where is bold Charlemagne?

Where the count dauphin of Auvergne? Where clever, good Bernard? Where the late John the First? But where is bold Charlemagne?
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad in Old French
translations.text:
For even the Holy Father, clad in amice and alb, girded with holy stoles that seize the wicked devil by the neck, dies as a layman dies: a gentle breeze carries him away; beings borne off by wind.

And Constantinople's lord in golden helm, or generous France's king who sowed churches and convents in God's honor and was our most glorious, though worshiped in their time, are beings borne off by wind.

Likewise the Dauphin of Vienne and Grenoble, prudent and fierce, or the Lord of Dijon, Salins, and Dole and his heir, or their people and courts, despite all they devoured, their squires and heralds, are beings borne off by wind.

Princes go to death like cleric and servant, and whether angry or sad, are beings borne off by wind.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad of the Women of Paris
translations.text:
Florentine and Venetian women have fine little mouths and may be procuresses, especially the old; beside Lombards, Romans, Genoese, Piedmontese, and Savoyards, Paris has the finest tongue. Neapolitans are famed for fair speech, they say; Germans and Prussians love cackling; Greek, Egyptian, Hungarian, Spanish, Catalan—Paris has the finest tongue. Bretons, Swiss, Gascons, women of Toulouse: two fishwives on the bridge silence them. Nor Portuguese, English, Calaisiennes, Picards, Valencians—Paris has the finest tongue.

Envoy

Prince, grant Parisian women the prize for speaking well; despite the Italians, Paris has the finest tongue.

Quatrain

I am François, which grieves me, born in Paris near Pontoise, and from a fathom of rope my neck will learn what my arse weighs.


Note: Poem written in prison, when Villon was sentenced to hang.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad and Prayer
translations.text:
Father Noah, who planted vines, and you, Lot, who drank so much in the cave that Love, ever full of traps, made you “know” your girls—not reproach, sweet innocent—and Architriclinus, certified drunkard, I pray you welcome grandly the soul of good Cotart, deceased.

Born long ago of your lineage, he drank the dearest and finest and excelled all at not paying. A bold knight of wine, he never trembled climbing barrels and fiercely defended his glass. Open Paradise's gates to the soul of good Cotart, deceased.

How often I saw the reveler stagger off to bed! Once he raised a bump striking a master butcher's stall. I doubt the world holds a man more enamored of wine. Let it enter when you hear it complain, the soul of good Cotart, deceased.

His spit never reached the ground. He cried, “My throat is on fire!” His soul could never quench its thirst, the soul of good Cotart, deceased.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad to His Lady for Robert d'Estouteville
translations.text:
At dawn, when the hawk stirs, moved by pleasure and nobility, the thrush leaps and cries joyfully, greeting his beloved in the brush, I wish to offer you—and tremble impatiently to do so—the sweetness due a lover. Know Love has written it in his book. This is the end to which God calls us.

You will always be mistress of my life, wholly, until my death: gentle laurel of my soul's dream, noble olive grove cooling Bitterness. Reason commands the fire endure (in this I follow its decree) that drives me toward you though it seem blind. This is the end to which God calls us.

When sorrow advances on me, when Fortune casts torment at me, your sweet, serene gaze dispels them as wind dispels smoke. I do not lose what I sow in you, for the fruit declares it will be mine. God asks it: I will keep cultivating you. This is the end to which God calls us. Hear, Princess, what my longing cries: my heart claims you forever. From you I hope the same constancy. This is the end to which God calls us.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad to His Lady
translations.text:
False beauty costing me so dear, truly harsh, hypocritical sweetness, love hard to gnaw and miserly, I may name you and death is certain, cowardly flower that pricks delightfully, mad pride firm in hanging, and icy eyes. Can Justice not rescue a poor man being killed?

I had better sought some garden of love elsewhere; that woman would have had no rival. Now I must flee, humiliated. Help! Help! Let someone aid me! If I must die, I will die fighting. May Pity, lacking at my cradle, rescue a poor man being killed.

The day will come when your fragrant flower is dry, withered, and faded. Though my laugh then seem a grimace, in old age it will triumph. I will be old, you ugly and wrinkled. Drink now while the stream is gentle! It will freeze, and warts cannot rescue a poor man being killed.

Prince of Love, exalted lover whom I do not wish to trouble: know nevertheless a good lord must rescue a poor man being killed.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad of Counter-Truths
translations.text:
There is no worry except when hungry; no service except an enemy's; no savor except a hay bale; no vigilance except a sleeping man's; no mercy except treason's; no safety except cowards'; no loyalty except the reformed man's; none wiser than the lover.

No begetting except in baths; no good fame except a shamed man's; no laughter except after a blow; no prestige except after denying debts; no true love except flattery; no good meeting except with wretches; no true report except a lie; none wiser than the lover.

No rest like living worried; no greater honor than saying bah; no vainglory except counterfeiters'; no health except a bloated man's; no high daring except cowardice; no reason except rage's; no sweetness except in a dazed woman; none wiser than the lover.

Would you hear the truth? No game except in sickness; no true word except in tragedy; no coward except the chivalrous; no horrible sound except melody; none wiser than the lover.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad of Good Doctrine
translations.text:
Whether you traffic forged pardons, cheat at dice, or counterfeit current coins like those who end scalded,* godless criminal and bandit, whether you swindle, rob, or commit adultery, where ends your ill-gotten gold? All goes to taverns and women.

Rhyme, mock, play an instrument like fools protected by disguise; turn clown or magician, invent a tale, stage mockeries, farces, and moralities wherever allowed, win at cards: all you acquire—listen and do not be angry—all goes to taverns and women.

Do such infamies repel you? Then plow fields and meadows, curry horses, asses, and mules if you are not learned, and you will earn enough. But if you are one of those who crush hemp, is it not true that the product of your arm all goes to taverns and women?

Hose, doublets, breeches, cloak, and every garment you have—take them, hurry, age escapes!—quickly to taverns, to women.


* “Scalded” refers to counterfeiters, for unauthorized coiners were put to death that way.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: The Replies to Franc Gontier
translations.text:
A fat priest sat on a soft bed beside the brazier in a matted room, Sidoine pressed to him kissing, tender, white, beautiful, adorned. Through a crack I saw them drink the best wine night and day, laugh, play, kiss, caress, both naked when they pleased, and learned that against bitterness no life is better than ease.

Had good Gontier and beloved Helen tried this life, they would not rub toast with garlic condemned by love. I value least their curds, stew, and creams. Sleep beneath a rosebush? I prefer a soft bed I can sink into. Is that not reason's choice? No life is better than ease.

They live on brown bread—madness!—and drink only water all year. I want none of the birds chirping in meadows at such a price, though they sing my favorite songs. Let Franc Gontier frolic with Helen beneath the insect-filled rosebush if they like that life. But I think: for happiness, no life is better than ease.

Prince, end this debate: I add that in my obscure childhood I heard a gaunt bard say, “No life is better than ease.”
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad of Fat Margot
translations.text:
If I love the beauty and serve her, does that alarm you? Do you deem me vile, foolish, witless? She has goods for every taste. For love of her I wear dagger and shield and kill. When someone comes I seize a jug and slip quietly from the room. Then I bring him cheese and bread, embrace him, and if he pays well say, “When will you return? When she is in heat, friend, we await you in the brothel where we earn our bread.”

But if dawn comes and he brought no money, woe to Margot! I rage, cannot look at her, want to cut her throat. I take her clothes outside and threaten to sell them. She stands like Antichrist, and I might kill her there, but by Christ's death she swears I will not. Thus we fight in the brothel where we earn our bread.

Then peace returns; she farts more criminally than a cannon shot, laughs and strikes me, then says, “Climb on!” as she settles. We sleep like clogs, both drunk. If she wakes and her belly still demands, she rises and mounts me. “She crushes us!” the bed and I groan, “Your lust breaks us apart!” in the brothel where we earn our bread.

Rain or thunder, my bread is secure. I am vicious and found a vicious woman. I swear I know not which is worse. Filth seems beautiful, honor disgusts us and we drive it away in the brothel where we earn our bread.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad
translations.text:
May envious tongues be fried in realgar* and arsenic oxide, yellow sulfide and quicklime, pitch and soot dissolved in lye made with urine and Jewish dung, boiling lead to crumble them, dirty leper-house water, foot scrapings and old clothes, asp's blood and various vipers, bile of wolves, foxes, and badgers!

May envious tongues be fried with brains of a cat too afraid of wet to fish, with rotten gums, or those of a mangy mastiff dripping rabid saliva, with pieces of a consumptive mule cooked in their own drool, in water where frogs, mice, toads, lizards, snakes, rats, and other noble beasts dip snout and mouth!

May envious tongues be fried in corrosive sublimate, dangerous to touch, on the navel of a living snake; in blood left in the barber's pots when the moon shines, one black, another dark green; in tubs where nurses scrape diapers and basins where venal nymphs wash—whoever does not understand me never went to brothels!

Prince, strain these dishes, if you have neither sieve nor screen, through the seats of dung-filled breeches, but first may envious tongues be fried in sow turds!


* Realgar, arsenic sulfide, a poisonous substance like orpiment (natural arsenic sulfide).
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad of Proverbs
translations.text:
The goat scratches until hurt; the pitcher goes to the well until it breaks; iron heats until red; it is struck until split; a man is worth as much as he is prized; he goes so far he is forgotten; becomes so bad he is despised; Christmas is invoked until it comes.

One speaks until contradicting himself; good fame is worth as much as favor gained; one promises until retracting; pleads until the thing is won; it is loved more the more it is sought; sought until found; more frequent the less desired; Christmas is invoked until it comes.

The dog is loved until fed; the song travels until learned; fruit is kept until rotten; a place besieged until conquered; delay ruins the venture; haste brings harm; one squeezes until the prize falls; Christmas is invoked until it comes.

One jokes until no laughter comes; spends until shirtless; gives so freely all is spent; taking is worth as much as promise; God is loved until church is followed; one gives until borrowing is needed; wind turns until north wind; Christmas is invoked until it comes.

Prince, a fool lives until cured, goes until returning, is beaten until changing his mind, Christmas is invoked until it comes.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Villon's Epitaph
translations.text:
O brothers living after us, do not close your merciful hearts, for if you pity our poor souls God will pity your eyes looking on us. Five or six hang here together; the flesh we fed at too much cost is long since gnawed and rotten, and we bones turn to ash and dust. Let none mock our misery: pray God absolve us all!

Do not disdain our cry, brothers, because justice put us to death. Understand not all know how to keep a serene spirit; forgive us now after death before the Virgin Mary's Son; seek that His grace not be denied and preserve us from infernal embers. We are dead; let none trouble us: pray God absolve us all!

Rain has strained and washed us; sun dried and blackened our trunks. Magpies and crows tore beard and brows and dug out our eyes. Never for an instant could we sit: here and there we swung at the wind's whim, dragged without cease, while birds pecked us more than sorghum. Let no one join our brotherhood: pray God absolve us all!

Prince Jesus, reigning over all, keep Hell from taking our souls: we have no business or debt in its mire. Men, this is no jest: pray God absolve us all!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad for Praying to Our Lady
translations.text:
Lady of heaven, Regent of earth, Empress of infernal marshes: receive this humble erring Christian; she longs to join your heavenly chosen though knowing she lacks such merit. The riches flowing from you, my Lady, exceed all my baseness. Without them no soul rises to heaven; I do not lie like minstrels: in this faith I wish to live and die.

Tell Your Son I seek his way. Ask him to erase my sins, to forgive me as Egyptian Mary or Theophilus the clerk, whose pact with the devil was pardoned through Your sweet smile's intercession. Preserve me from the ever-stirring demon, Virgin who conceived without stain the sacrament celebrated at Mass: in this faith I wish to live and die.

I am poor and old and know no sacred texts, but in the church where I go for aid I saw Eden painted with harps and lutes and Hell where the damned boil. One greatly frightens me; my eyes joyfully behold the other, the only truth I know. I dream of reaching that bliss one day, Lady to whom sinners must turn sincerely, promptly, faithfully: in this faith I wish to live and die.

Your holy pregnancy, worthy Virgin Princess, bore King Jesus, infinite and unceasing, who assumed our sad nature, left heaven and came to die for us, sacrificing youthful beauty. Such is our God. My soul confesses itself His: in this faith I wish to live and die.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Ballad of the Ladies of Former Times
translations.text:
Tell me in what land, tell me where to find Flora, Roman beauty; where Archipiada hides from light and Thaïs, her cousin; Echo, condemned afar to repeat water's song and mountain's noise, so beautiful when fate wished; but where have last year's snows gone?

Tell where wise Héloïse is, for whom learned Abelard was castrated and then cloistered at famous Saint-Denis, paying thus for reckless passion. Where too is the queen who had Buridan, her lover, thrown into the Seine in a sack? But where have last year's snows gone?

Queen Blanche, white as fleur-de-lis, who sang with false siren voice; Bertha Big-Foot, Beatrice, Alice, Haremburg who ruled all Maine, and Lorraine's good, brave Joan, burned at Rouen by the outlaw Englishman—Sovereign Virgin, where are they kept? But where have last year's snows gone?

Prince, search neither year nor week for the hidden place they escaped without my refrain singing in your ear: “But where have last year's snows gone?”
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: In My Backpack...
translations.text:
In my backpack
a little thyme stem
two coins
a blunt pencil
crumpled notes
cookie crumbs
a green clothespin
the business card of a Japanese Germanist
a small toothless comb
Dalí's ants on a sheet of music.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Hieroglyphs of Love
translations.text:
Hieroglyphs of love
Natalia vanished
stonecutter at the primal work
time the grand Methodist
a herd assaults with waving voices
turning toward his face
to his cotton arm
soft beardless armchair
possessed by the black and light:
“In the homeland it is beautiful...”
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: My Dear Feather-Eyed One!
translations.text:
My dear feather-eyed one!
My shackled little lookout lock!
My enchanting anemone
how you have abandoned me
and now I must weep for you.

White anemone
little April
distant springing water of my heart
fifteenth little key of my grief.
Farewell, you go into spring green!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly for batch completion; no separate editorial review was performed.

translations.title: Better to Travel in Thought, Hokusai
translations.text:
On one's back, or beneath the lamp
run to Fuji's foot and look upward
at the snowy peak, the snow boots
wet and cold, the wilted collar.
How, I ask, to investigate distance
with one's own feet, how, I ask, to experience distance
with one's own eyes. How to join longing for distance
with staying still. How, feet and eyes,
tears and pleasure.

translations.title: The Sacred Image Has...
translations.text:
The sacred image has
a blue thorn.
Jesus is baptized
in orange. Almost beyond
again and again the Last Judgment.
Blessed ones who smile and
form choirs. Pale green
the earth sinks, but
the heavens soon grow calm.
Brighter, they wave like silver
flags in slow motion,
and the tallest candle strives
and gives off scent.
I stand before you in cold dust
I stand before you from somewhere
from a frozen darkness
I stand before you and sing praise:
gazes of praise lifted me
from the weary stirrups of my
feeling, without a murmur.
